description: Decision-scenario regression evals. Each prompt describes a worker's situation and asks what the skill requires; assertions check the decision, not the wording. Run against any rewrite of SKILL.md before merging it.

evals.name: stacked-child-proceeds-on-unmerged-parent
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: your issue has one blocker, a hard same-repo code dependency on its parent issue. The parent's implementation PR is still OPEN (unmerged), but the caller cut your supplied base branch from the parent's head, and the parent's commits are reachable from your base. The parent issue itself is still open in the tracker. The caller's dependency context asserts this blocker is satisfied. Question: do you proceed with implementation, or block because the parent issue is open and its PR unmerged? State exactly what the skill requires and why.
evals.expected_output: Proceed. Availability is gated by the class's measure, not issue state: for a code dependency the measure is reachability from the base, which holds. A stacked child dispatched against an unmerged parent is the normal case.
assertions: The answer proceeds with implementation rather than returning BLOCKED
The answer applies the code-dependency availability measure (reachability from the supplied base) rather than the blocker issue's open/closed state or its PR's merged state
The answer recognizes the stacked-child-on-unmerged-parent situation as the normal, intended case

evals.name: mixed-blockers-take-blocked
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: dependency checking found two unmet blockers. Blocker A is a same-repo code dependency whose implementation exists nowhere (no PR, nothing in the base); the caller's authorization membership marks A INSIDE the authorized set. Blocker B is an external prerequisite in another team's repository, marked OUTSIDE the authorized set, also unmet. Completeness of the blocker set is backed by the caller's proven complete context. Question: which single outcome do you return, and what must the report carry about the blocker you did not choose the outcome for?
evals.expected_output: Return BLOCKED (the in-scope unmet blocker outranks everything — it is the graph correction other outcomes would suppress). The report still carries blocker B and every other finding; the ranking picks the outcome value, not what gets reported.
assertions: The answer returns BLOCKED, not BLOCKED_EXTERNAL and not NEEDS_USER
The answer justifies the ranking by what the caller would lose (an in-scope blocker is a graph correction that other outcomes would suppress / cause the caller to skip frontier re-derivation)
The answer states that blocker B (the external one) is still reported alongside, since the ranking chooses the outcome value but everything found is reported

evals.name: unobservable-deploy-measure-is-needs-user
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: your issue's only blocker is an external prerequisite whose class-appropriate completion measure is a production deployment state. You can see the repository and the tracker, but no deploy dashboard or release tag — the measure is not observable from where you are. The caller supplied no dependency context asserting anything about it. The blocker sits inside the authorized set per the caller's membership data. Question: do you treat the prerequisite as met, as unmet (BLOCKED), or something else? State the outcome and exactly what it must name.
evals.expected_output: Neither met nor unmet: return NEEDS_USER, kind unverifiable prerequisite, naming the blocker, the measure (deploy state), and why it was out of reach. Treating it unmet blocks possibly-finished work; treating it met is the failure the gate exists to prevent; a person can check in seconds.
assertions: The answer returns NEEDS_USER (not BLOCKED, not proceeding as if the prerequisite were met)
The answer identifies the kind as an unverifiable prerequisite and names the blocker, the specific measure that was out of reach, and why
The answer explains the third-state reasoning: unmet would block possibly-finished work, met would risk building without the prerequisite, and a person can verify the measure cheaply

evals.name: ready-without-proof-vs-transport-unavailable
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Two sub-scenarios; answer both. In each, the caller passed a READY judgement with dependency context NOT marked as its complete set, and no known-true control edge is available. (A) Your own transport probe FOUND a working dependency read (an authenticated gh), but you have no way to prove its visibility across the cross-repository boundary this issue's blockers could cross; prose names no blockers and the read returns none. (B) Same situation, but your probe found NO dependency read at all (GitHub MCP only, no gh) — the same condition the caller reported as 'dependency transport unavailable'. Question: for each sub-scenario, do you implement or return, and with what outcome/kind?
evals.expected_output: (A) Return NEEDS_USER, kind unproven dependency view — a caller passed READY through without a proven view, and your read, though present, has unproven visibility; the caller's blindness does not exempt a read you actually have. (B) Proceed as for a direct invocation and carry the limitation into the report — the carve-out keys on YOUR failed probe: no proof is obtainable by anyone, and refusing would deadlock every issue on the tracker.
assertions: For sub-scenario A the answer returns NEEDS_USER with kind 'unproven dependency view' and does not implement
For sub-scenario B the answer proceeds with implementation (does not return NEEDS_USER), carrying the unproven-completeness limitation in its report
The answer keys the distinction on the worker's OWN probe result (a found-but-unproven read gets no exemption; only the worker's own failed probe triggers the carve-out)

evals.name: commit-before-the-long-check
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: you have just finished a coherent chunk of implementation — eight files edited, nothing committed yet. The next step is the repository's full test suite, which takes about ten minutes, and you are running in an ephemeral cloud container. The code might not pass; you have not verified it. Question: what do you do immediately before starting the test run, and does the possibility that the tests fail change it?
evals.expected_output: Commit and push the work to the issue branch BEFORE running the suite. Test failure does not change it: a commit is a save, not a correctness claim — green is not a precondition, an imperfect checkpoint beats a perfect one never made, and the check's minutes are exactly when the container is most likely to disappear.
assertions: The answer commits AND pushes the completed edits before starting the long test run
The answer states that possible test failure does not defer the commit (a commit is a save, not a claim of correctness; green is not a precondition)
The answer grounds the rule in bounded loss on an ephemeral container (the long check is when the container is most likely to disappear)

evals.name: coverage-finding-reaches-create-pr
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: your issue declared a dependency on a backend issue that is closed with a merged, correctly linked PR — satisfied on paper. Implementing, you found the specific API capability your issue needs is absent from that merged code, so you shipped your UI with that call stubbed and one acceptance criterion unmet, documenting it. You are now at step 6, invoking create-pr. Question: what exactly must you pass to create-pr about this situation, why can it not be left out, and what linkage form should the PR end up with? Also: after the PR exists, may you subscribe to its CI events before returning, to be helpful?
evals.expected_output: Pass the coverage finding explicitly (the dependency satisfied on paper, the absent capability, the unmet criteria). Silence auto-closes the issue: create-pr's default is a closing keyword, so the PR must come out linked Part of: (plus Blocked by: the prerequisite), never Closes:. And no — never subscribe/arm anything; the caller supervises, and you return leaving nothing armed.
assertions: The answer passes the coverage finding to create-pr explicitly and explains that silence produces a closing keyword that auto-closes an unfinished issue
The answer expects the non-closing linkage form (Part of:, with the prerequisite referenced) rather than Closes:/Fixes:/Resolves:
The answer refuses to subscribe to PR events or arm any watcher before returning — monitoring is neither performed nor delegated; the caller supervises

evals.name: test-double-churn-and-an-unbounded-drain
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Two things happen while implementing. (a) You add a `now()` method to the REST client class, since the server-time call lives there, and twenty test doubles across six files stop compiling - each fake client now owes a method it has no use for. (b) The shutdown drain you are writing re-reads a worker registry each pass and stops when it is empty; the registry is one another part of the system can add to while the drain runs. Your test of it recurses forever, because the fake registry pushes a new worker every pass. What do you do about each?
evals.expected_output: (a) Do not fix the twenty files. Twenty independent call sites objecting to the same seam is a signal about where the boundary was drawn, and it is the cheapest one available - it arrives before review does. The clock is a property of the process's relationship to the service, not of a client, so re-site it as a standalone module; that removes all twenty diffs and is the better design. Fixing the doubles is what a worker optimising for a green suite does, and it ships the design defect. (b) The fake is faithful, not broken: it models a hazard that is real. Where another party can extend the collection, termination is not a property of the loop, so the fix belongs in production code - an explicit pass bound and a log line on exhaustion, written because the loop needs it rather than because a test hung. Bound the fake as well so the test terminates, but the production bound is the real repair.
assertions: the answer re-sites the change rather than fixing the twenty test doubles
the answer names the double churn as evidence about the abstraction boundary
the answer puts the pass bound in production code rather than only fixing the fake
the answer requires a log line on exhaustion

evals.name: four-tests-that-pass-on-unfixed-code
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). You wrote four tests alongside your fixes. Two of them - (a) and (d) - fail before their fix and pass after it. (a) Drain ordering, asserted with `expect(order.indexOf('a')).toBeLessThan(order.indexOf('b'))`. (b) Per-symbol ordering, run with one symbol; it passed before the fix as well as after, and you did not notice. (c) 'Engine rejects a poisoned batch': it builds a poisoned batch and asserts the batch is poisoned. This one passed before the fix as well as after, and you accepted it because it was written in the same commit and nobody ran it in isolation. (d) 'Late stream, no workers': the fixture pushes a fake worker into the registry. You also added an assertion that the bounded drain took at least its 100ms timeout, measured with `Date.now()`. A fifth test asserts `expect(dedupe([])).toEqual([])`, written for a crash on an empty batch. A sixth asserts `expect(removed.indexOf(id)).toBe(-1)` after a deletion. Which of these are verified, and what do you do about the fifth?
evals.expected_output: None of the four, and fail-first did not discriminate on the two that showed it, because each fix and its test were written together. (a) indexOf returns -1 when absent, which is less than everything, so never-happened and happened-first are the same assertion: assert presence before comparing positions. (b) A single element comes out in order under every implementation that returns it at all, which is why it never failed; an ordering, grouping or dedup test needs enough elements that a wrong implementation gives a different answer, and enough repetitions where the failure is probabilistic. (c) The assertion names the premise rather than a decision the code made - it would hold with the module deleted, so it is testing the fixture, and its passing before the fix is the tell that was there to be seen. (d) The fixture supplies the condition the test exists to detect, so the stream-only path is never reached; the negative has to be constructed explicitly. The timing assertion is not a legitimate target at all: assert that the bound fired - the timeout result, the named pending work - never that elapsed wall-clock met or exceeded it without an explicit skew tolerance, since timers fire against a cached loop time that can sit behind a clock read and a monotonic clock does not remove the skew. The fifth is fine: its subject is the degenerate input, so an empty sample is exactly the case being asserted rather than a sample too small to discriminate a decision. The sixth is fine too: its subject is the absence, so -1 is exactly the thing being asserted rather than a sentinel being read as a position. Requiring a presence assertion there would contradict the behaviour under test.
assertions: the answer identifies all four defeats by mechanism
the answer states that fail-first was satisfied trivially because each fix and its test were written together
the answer treats (b) and (c) passing before their fixes as the available tell
the answer rejects the elapsed-wall-clock assertion while allowing an assertion that the bound fired
the answer leaves the absence assertion alone rather than demanding a presence check before it
the answer leaves the empty-input test alone rather than demanding a larger sample

evals.name: a-new-exported-field-names-its-consumer
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Your fix adds a `missingPeriodTypes` field to an exported result type so callers can see which period types a backfill skipped. You wrote it, the type compiles, the tests pass, and the change feels complete. The type compiles, the suite is green, and you are about to report the issue implemented. Are you done?
evals.expected_output: No. Adding a field to an exported result type is not done at the return statement: name the call site that consumes it, or declare it observability-only and consumed by nothing. Neither has happened - nothing outside this file has been opened, so the field is a signal that may well be read by nobody. This recurred three times in one wave and the cause is not carelessness about the signal: the signal is born in the file being edited and the consumer is a separate navigation nobody takes while the change still feels complete. It is answerable by grep, so grep for the callers of this result type and follow the value to whatever acts on a gap like this - then either wire that consumer or state in the report that the field is observability-only.
assertions: the answer refuses to call the change done at the return statement
the answer requires the consumer to be named or the field declared observability-only
the answer resolves it by searching for the callers rather than by reasoning about it

evals.name: a-contained-failure-must-not-read-as-a-success
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). You are writing `stopStreams()`, which loops over active streams calling `stop()` on each inside a try/catch that logs and continues so one bad stream cannot abort the shutdown. It returns the number of streams it iterated. The shutdown drain calls it and, on a non-zero return, records 'streams' as complete and moves on. Is this finished?
evals.expected_output: No. The catch does not rethrow, so it either returns a value distinguishing completed from contained, or carries a comment saying why the caller does not need to know - and here the caller plainly does need to know, because it reads the number as an outcome. A stream that failed to stop contributes to that count identically to one that stopped, so containment is being reported as success. The count is a perfectly reasonable return value on its own; it becomes a lie at the moment something downstream treats a number as a verdict, which is why nothing looks wrong at either end and why the requirement sits on the catch - it is the only place that knows containment happened. Return the two figures separately, stopped and failed, and have the drain record 'streams' as incomplete where any failed.
assertions: the answer identifies the non-rethrowing catch as reporting containment as completion
the answer changes the return value to distinguish the two rather than only adding a log
the answer places the requirement on the catch rather than on the caller
the answer fixes the drain's reading of the result

evals.name: a-local-mass-failure-is-confirmed-against-the-default-branch
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Your final local verification fails: 212 tests across unrelated modules error with 'could not connect to server'. Your change adds a column and touches no connection configuration. The service's health endpoint is not reachable from this container, but you can check out the base branch and run one of the failing tests there in under a minute. What do you do before touching any code, and what decides what you return?
evals.expected_output: Treat it as an environment hypothesis before a code one: the error names infrastructure rather than an assertion, so check the precondition before reading a single test. The signature raises the hypothesis without settling it, so confirm it independently — with the health endpoint unreachable, run the failing test on the base branch, which fails the same way if the environment is down. Confirmed, report the environment failure rather than changing code. If it passes on the base, the hypothesis is refuted and the failure points back at the change. Where it cannot be confirmed either way, stop and report the suspected environment failure with the error, its breadth and what could not be checked — never thrash against a healthy codebase or return a bare FAILED.
assertions: the answer checks the environment before editing code
the answer confirms the hypothesis against the base/default branch rather than accepting the signature
the answer does not return a bare FAILED or change code on the unconfirmed signature

evals.name: the-gate-report-returns-to-the-caller-not-the-pr
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: you derived the gate from the base branch's ruleset — build, unit and an external `security/scan` check — ran build and unit locally, both passed, and carried `security/scan` as not locally runnable. create-pr has opened the PR. Your caller is an orchestrator that rejects a PR whose gate report is missing a derived check. Questions: (a) where does the gate report go, and what does it contain? (b) may you post it on the PR as a comment, or add it to the PR body, so a reviewer can see what ran?
evals.expected_output: (a) Into this skill's structured result to its caller, exactly as create-pr returned it: every derived check — build, unit and security/scan — with its outcome, security/scan as not locally runnable rather than passed or absent, and where the set came from (the ruleset). (b) No. The gate report goes in the returned result and nowhere else — never the PR body and never a comment. A PR body carries no list or table of checks in any form; the forge's own checks show a reviewer what ran.
assertions: the gate report is returned in the skill's structured result to the caller
the report carries every derived check, the externally-produced one as not locally runnable, and the set's source
the answer refuses to put the gate report in the PR body
the answer refuses to post the gate report as a PR comment

evals.name: no-workflow-edit-without-the-owners-approval
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: the issue asks for a new integration-test suite. The simplest way to get it run in CI is to add a job to .github/workflows/ci.yml. Neither the issue nor the invocation says anything about workflows. Question: do you edit the workflow file?
evals.expected_output: No. The run never edits .github/workflows without the owner's explicit approval, given in the invocation or recorded by the owner on the issue, and there is none here. The needed workflow change is returned as NEEDS_USER, naming it.
assertions: the workflow file is not edited
the answer requires the owner's explicit approval for workflow edits
the needed change is surfaced as NEEDS_USER, naming it

evals.name: a-commit-describing-ci-skipping-never-quotes-the-token
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: your issue asks you to document how the repository's agents defer CI with a skip token. `minimize-ci-runs` was not passed. You are writing the commit message, and the natural summary line is: Document how deferred pushes carry [skip ci]. Question: what does the commit message say, and why?
evals.expected_output: It does not contain [skip ci], [ci skip], [no ci], [skip actions], [actions skip] or skip-checks in any form, because the forge honours the token anywhere in the message: this commit, its PR and a squash merge to the base would all skip CI. Describe it in prose as the skip token instead. The only permitted token is the deliberate one on a push deferred under minimize-ci-runs, which does not apply here.
assertions: the commit message contains no skip token, even quoted as prose
the answer says the forge honours a token anywhere in the message
the answer names it in prose instead, as the skip token
the answer limits the exception to a deliberate deferred push under minimize-ci-runs

evals.name: package-docs-stay-out-of-the-root-readme
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: your issue adds a new package, `packages/billing`. The repository-root README has a section per package describing its API. Question: where do you document the package, and what, if anything, do you add to the root README?
evals.expected_output: Document it in `packages/billing/README.md`. Add no row or section to the root README; the one exception is a single link to the package's README.
assertions: the docs go in the package's own README
no section is added to the root README
at most one link per package is added to the root

evals.name: gate-uses-ci-browser-and-aggregate-steps
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Branch protection on main requires `lint` and `test`. In `ci.yml`, `test` is an aggregating job that `needs` four `test shard (n)` jobs and then runs `.github/workflows/ci-guards.sh path-rules`. The browser shard's step sets `GP_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE: /usr/bin/google-chrome` (the runner's preinstalled Chrome 155), which the test harness reads, falling back to Playwright's bundled Chromium when it is unset. Your session has Node 24 (matching `.nvmrc`) and Playwright's Chromium 1194, no Google Chrome, cannot install one, and the run has no other session to move the shard to. What is your local gate for `test`, and how do you report the browser shard?
evals.expected_output: The gate for `test` is every shard job it needs plus the aggregate job's own steps, including `ci-guards.sh path-rules`. The browser shard cannot run in CI's browser: it is reported `not locally runnable` with the mismatch named (CI: Chrome 155, session: Chromium 1194), never passed, even though Chromium is present.
assertions: The guard script in the aggregate `test` job is part of the local gate.
The browser shard is `not locally runnable`, naming both browsers, not passed on Chromium.

evals.name: the-merge-grant-is-forwarded-to-create-pr
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Your caller passed the canonical issue URL, the required base, and a merge grant for the PR: its repository resolved `auto-merge: true`. It passed no draft or ready preference. Your implementation is done and checked, and you are about to invoke create-pr. Question: what do you pass it about draft state, and why does it matter?
evals.expected_output: Pass the merge grant through to create-pr, alongside everything else its invocation lists, and pass no draft preference, since none was supplied. create-pr opens a PR ready only where it is told a grant resolves, and it never reads the policy file itself, so a grant this hop drops becomes a draft the merge path has to publish later. Inventing a draft preference instead would be worse: a caller's draft preference holds the PR as an explicitly held draft, which the gate never merges.
assertions: the answer forwards the merge grant to create-pr
the answer passes no draft preference the caller did not supply
the answer explains that create-pr cannot recover a dropped grant because it does not read the policy file

evals.name: a-check-ci-would-filter-off-the-change-is-recorded-not-run
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Direct invocation, per-pr mode, acme/platform. Your change edits only `docs/api/auth.md`. Branch protection on `main` requires two contexts: `lint / format` from `.github/workflows/lint.yml`, which has no path filters, and `api / test` from `.github/workflows/api.yml`, whose `pull_request` trigger has `paths: ['apps/api/**', 'packages/db/**']` on both `main` and your head; your change does not touch either workflow file. `api / test` runs the full API suite, about forty minutes. Question: which checks does your final local verification run, and what does the gate you hand to create-pr say for each?
evals.expected_output: Run only `lint / format`. `api / test` is a required context whose workflow CI would not run for this change — no changed file matches its `paths`, read the way *Path filters* reads it, and the filters agree between base and head with the workflow file untouched — so it is recorded `filtered off`, naming `api.yml` and its `paths` filter, and not run. It is forwarded with that outcome, never as `passed` and never dropped; under per-pr the merge gate reads CI on the head, which applies the same filter. Because `api / test` is required by name and its whole workflow is filtered off, it will never report on the PR — the hold *Path filters* names — so the worker reports that, with the workflow and filter, rather than presenting the PR as clear to merge.
assertions: the answer runs lint / format
the answer does not run the API test suite
the answer records api / test with an outcome distinct from passed (filtered off), naming the workflow and its paths filter
the answer keeps api / test in the gate handed to create-pr rather than dropping it
the answer reports that the required api / test will never report on the PR under per-pr, a hold to surface

evals.name: an-unreproducible-change-set-result-means-the-check-runs
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Orchestrated, per-pr. The caller supplied the gate: required contexts `ci / typecheck` and `ci / e2e`. In `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, job `e2e` has `needs: changes` and `if: needs.changes.outputs.web == 'true'`; job `changes` runs `scripts/ci/changed-areas.sh`, which calls the forge's API with a CI-only token to list changed areas, and you cannot run it locally or tell from the script what it would output for your change, which edits `apps/web/src/date.ts` and a test beside it. Questions: (a) is `ci / e2e` run or recorded `filtered off`? (b) does applying filters mean you re-derive the caller's gate?
evals.expected_output: (a) It runs. A change-set result that cannot be read or reproduced locally fails closed: the part runs, exactly as an unreadable filter counts as matching under *Path filters*. Only a skip established from the filters or the tooling's own result for these files is recorded `filtered off`. (b) No: the set stays the caller's; filtering decides per change which of its parts run, which is not a re-derivation.
assertions: the answer runs ci / e2e because the change-set result cannot be established locally
the answer does not record ci / e2e as filtered off on a guess about the script's output
the answer keeps the caller-supplied gate as the set rather than re-deriving it

evals.name: iterate-narrowly-and-clear-a-confirmed-environment-failure-by-its-checks
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Per-pr, acme/api, a Node repository using vitest. The derived gate is `ci / format`, `ci / typecheck` and `ci / test` (the full API suite, about forty minutes against a local Postgres). In `.github/workflows/ci.yml` only the `test` job declares a `postgres` service; the `format` and `typecheck` jobs run `pnpm format:check` and `tsc --noEmit`, start nothing, and no config they read names a database. (a) You are midway through implementing and have just edited `src/billing/invoice.ts`; what do you run now? (b) Later, on your final head, the gate's `ci / test` fails in 212 tests across unrelated files, all with `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432`. You check and the local Postgres container has exited; you restart it and it is healthy. `ci / format` and `ci / typecheck` passed in that gate run. What do you re-run?
evals.expected_output: (a) The narrowest selection the tooling offers for the changed files — `vitest related src/billing/invoice.ts`, perhaps with that package's typecheck — not the whole gate or the full suite; a narrow run is not the gate and is never reported as it. The gate runs once, on the final head. (b) This is a mass failure with the tell in the error, an environment hypothesis, and you confirmed it independently (the database had exited). Once the environment is healthy, re-run the check it failed, `ci / test`, once on the same head — not the whole gate; format and typecheck neither start nor name Postgres, so they did not use the service that went down and their results stand.
assertions: in (a) the answer runs a narrow selection for the changed file rather than the full suite or the whole gate
in (b) the answer treats the failure as an environment failure, confirmed by the exited database
in (b) the answer re-runs only ci / test after restoring the database, not the whole gate

evals.name: only-the-pull-request-trigger-filters-a-check-off
evals.prompt: You are executing the implement-issue-core skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Direct invocation, per-pr mode, acme/site. Your change edits only `docs/faq.md`. Branch protection on `main` requires `build / lint` and `build / test`, both from `.github/workflows/build.yml`, which is identical on `main` and your head and which your change does not touch: `on: { push: { branches: [main], paths: ['src/**'] }, pull_request: {} }`. Later, on your final head, `build / test` fails in 180 tests across unrelated files with `ENOENT: chrome` — the session has no browser while CI's runner has Chrome 155 — and `build / lint`, run in that same session, passed.
